Roughhead grenadier (Macrourus berglax) attains a maximum recorded total length of 110 cm [Li = 110 cm], which represents the largest individuals documented in trawl surveys across the Northwest Atlantic. This ultimate size is notably greater than that observed in several congeneric species, including Macrourus carinatus, which typically does not exceed 90 cm. The species displays pronounced sexual dimorphism, with mature females generally reaching larger dimensions than males of equivalent age. Analysis of otolith-derived age estimates suggests that growth decelerates markedly after sexual maturation, with most somatic expansion occurring during the first decade of life. The body plan of this benthopelagic grenadier is characterized by a long, tapering tail and a relatively large head, traits well suited to its deep-water habitat where scavenging and predation on benthic invertebrates dominate the feeding ecology. Specimens approaching 110 cm [Li = 110 cm] are exceptionally rare in commercial bycatch, likely reflecting either natural mortality prior to attaining this size or a skewed population structure resulting from selective fishing pressure on larger individuals. Nevertheless, the species' pronounced longevity and slow growth rate render it particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as population recovery from depletion would require several decades under the coldest thermal regimes encountered at depth.

This low fecundity is partially offset by the production of large, yolk-rich eggs that yield well-provisioned neonates. The estimated maximum reproductive rate translates to approximately 0.6 eggs per day, a value consistent with the low metabolic rates documented in other macrourids inhabiting the Labrador Sea and Davis Strait. This strategy prioritizes offspring quality over quantity, a common adaptive response to the unpredictable food supply and high energy costs of reproduction in deep-water ecosystems.
